articles.title: FACT CHECK: Unrelated audio used in video of crowd mocking VP Sara in Hong Kong
articles.summary: The audio of a chant calling the Vice President a thief was taken from a July 2026 rally in Manila and added to the video circulating online

blocks.text: Claim: A video shows overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) chanting a song with the lyrics “Sara Sara Magnanakaw” (Sara, Sara is a thief) during Vice President Sara Duterte’s visit to Hong Kong.
Why we fact-checked this: The claim appears in a video shared in multiple Facebook posts on November 8 by various pages and accounts, including the following:

items: A post from the page “Pro Filipinas,” with around 25,400 reactions, 7,400 comments, 4,200 shares, and 700,000 views as of writing
A post from the account “Nhenz Ros,” with around 10,500 reactions, 3,100 comments, 1,700 shares, and 269,000 views as of writing
Posts on November 8 from the account “Yayam Dizon,” the account “Anna Belle,” the page “Kagawad Joey,” and the page “Venus Domingo Dugam.”

blocks.text: The facts: The video showing a crowd seemingly calling Duterte a thief used audio from a different, unrelated source: a video titled “Sara, Sara magnanakaw” posted on July 6 on the YouTube channel and Facebook page of Abante News Online.

The Abante News Online video showed protesters chanting the exact same lyrics and in the same tone in front of the Senate building. July 6 was the first day of Duterte’s impeachment trial. (READ: Inside the courtroom: Week 1 of Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial)
Other videos from Duterte’s meeting with OFWs in Hong Kong do not show the crowd singing the song.

Duterte traveled to Hong Kong from November 6 to 8 “to attend engagements and participate in various activities, including an event organized by the Filipino community,” according to a statement released by the Office of the Vice President.

Impeachment trial updates: The impeachment trial of the Vice President resumed on Monday, November 9, following a nearly monthlong break. It is currently the turn of the defense, led by counsel Sheila Sison, to present its evidence and witnesses. (READ: Sara Duterte trial: Defense begins presentation of evidence)

On October 13, the last trial date before the break, the prosecution dropped three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Duterte — the articles on alleged confidential fund misuse, bribery, and grave threats — leaving only the unexplained wealth case to expedite the proceedings.

On November 5, the Senate impeachment court confirmed admitting the prosecution’s evidence against Duterte, overruling the defense’s objections regarding the admissibility and relevance of the prosecution’s documentary evidence. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte)
Previous related fact-checks: Rappler has fact-checked numerous videos containing audio later determined to be superimposed on unrelated video, such as in the following fact-checks:

items: FACT CHECK: ‘Duterte’ chants in video are manipulated, not taken in Netherlands (March 13, 2025)
FACT CHECK: Duterte chants fabricated in video of Alyansa slate rally (February 20, 2025)
FACT CHECK: ‘Duterte!’ chants fabricated in video of Pope Francis’ East Timor visit (September 16, 2024)
MANIPULADONG BIDYO: Kinanta ang isang UniTeam chant sa BTS concert (March 23, 2022)
FALSE: Cebuanos scream ‘Fuck you’ at Bongbong Marcos during his visit (October 26, 2021)

blocks.text: Rappler has also fact-checked several false claims regarding Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial. – Percival Bueser/Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte's 'loose investment' still business participation -- UP law expert
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte having a "loose investment" may still be considered participating in a business and transacting with that entity, according to a law expert.

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 3:41pm
Vice President Sara Duterte having a "loose investment" may still be considered participating in a business and transacting with that entity, according to a law expert.
Defense witness Suzette Balucanag-Punay, an in-house counsel for GenCorp. Industries Inc., said Duterte had a "loose investment" in one of five fast food branches owned by the firm.

Punay said the vice president did not receive dividends from 2022 to 2025 since there were no dividends declared by the company. What she received from GenCorp, Punay said, was monthly payouts as "return of capital" from 2022 to 2025 amounting to P2.14 million.

Speaking with GMA News during an intermission of the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, Paolo Tamase, associate dean of University of the Philippines College of Law, said the admission from the defense's own witnesses pointed to regular transactions between Duterte and GenCorp.

"Sinabi ng GenCorp witness today na wala namang dividend na in-issue 'yung GenCorp. If this pertains to the 'loose investment' na tinatawag nila, that is still arguably participation in business and hindi puwede i-downplay 'yung danger of not declaring these types of transactions, especially for officers with a history of local government," Tamase said.

(The GenCorp witness said today that what GenCorp issued did not have dividends. If this pertains to the 'loose investment' that they are saying, that is still arguably participation in business and the danger of not declaring these types of transactions could not be downplayed, especially for officers with a history of local government.)

"If the vice president, in fact had investments na hindi kasama sa SALN, and 'yung admissions na 'yun ay coming from their own witnesses, I think there's a case that this may even be worse than what the prosecution had already presented," he added, referring to the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

(If the vice president, in fact, had investments that are not included in the SALN, and those admissions came from their own witness, I think there's a case that this may even be worse than what the prosecution had already presented.)
The disclosure of these details is important, Tamase explained.
Since these high-ranking officials are so entrenched in government, Tamase said, they are prevented from engaging in opportunities to engage in a business where they can profit from.
Cabrera's findings

The prosecution had wrapped up their presentation of witnesses with financial forensic analyst lawyer Alexander Cabrera, who presented a report saying that Duterte had at least some P817 million in unexplained wealth.
Cabrera had testified that Duterte has 20% ownership of GenCorp, citing market research and corporate records.
Tamase said Punay's admission of these investments that were not on the SALN and could add to the P817 million flagged by Cabrera.

"If 'yung sarili nilang witnesses nagsasabi na mayroon siyang investments in individual branches and at least one individual branch, and then una, hindi ganoon kadali mawalang bisa or ipa-deny 'yung allegations ni Atty. Cabrera because it seems to be kahit denied 'yung GenCorp investment, apparently may investment in a branch owned by GenCorp, so may truth to it actually, 'yung sinasabi nung testigo," Tamase said.

(If their own witness would say that she has investments in individual branches and at least one individual branch, then first, it is not so easy to invalidate or deny the allegations of Atty. Cabrera because even if GenCorp denies the investment, apparently there is still an investment in a branch owned by GenCorp, so there is some truth to what the witness was saying.)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.title: US warns Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia
articles.summary: US general warns the Sahel model-like security deal with Russia could lead to greater instability in Africa.

blocks.text: The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.
US Africa Command deputy head Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade.
He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent.
Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have severed ties with the Western partners and turned to Russia to military support their fight against jihadist groups.
Russia has expanded its military cooperation with Madagascar since the military seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors.
"We are concerned about Russia wanting to "proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent", Brennan told reporters in an online briefing.
"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.
The three Sahel countries had blamed their former Western partners for failing to contain jihadist violence before turning to Moscow.
However, militant attacks have continued despite their closer military ties with Russia.
Brennan also raised concerns about security in the Mozambique Channel, which separates Mozambique and Madagascar from mainland Africa and is an important route for international shipping and trade.
He said it was vital to prevent Islamist State linked militants in northern Mozambique and other hostile actors from threatening maritime activity.
Citing recent piracy-related incidents along the coast, Brennan said militant groups in northern Mozambique were adapting their tactics, including developing greater maritime capabilities.
He said US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish" but urged them to understand the potential risks.
Madagascar has not publicly responded to Brennan's comments,.
However, President Michaël Randrianirina has recently reiterated his support for stronger ties between Russia and African countries.
During the Russia-Africa summit last month, Madagascar and Russia signed several cooperation agreements covering defence, tourism and trade.
In February, a few months after taking power in a military takeover, Randrianirina visited to Moscow. It was the first official visit to Russia by a Malagasy leader in nearly 50 years.

articles.title: Globe spends P35.8B in first 9 months of 2026 to improve network
articles.summary: Ayala-led Globe Telecom Inc. spent P35.8 billion on capital expenditures (capex) in the first nine months of 2026, ramping up investments to strengthen its network infrastructure and expand its…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 3:22pm

Ayala-led Globe Telecom Inc. spent P35.8 billion on capital expenditures (capex) in the first nine months of 2026, ramping up investments to strengthen its network infrastructure and expand its digital capabilities nationwide.
In a disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange, Globe said its capex spending from January to September was 14% higher than the amount recorded in the same period last year.
The nine-month spending was equivalent to 28% of the telecommunications company's service revenues.

Globe said 89% of its capital outlays went to data-related requirements, focusing on improving network performance, accommodating rising data consumption and expanding capacity to meet the evolving digital needs of consumers and businesses.
The higher investments coincided with growth in Globe's top line, driven by sustained demand across its mobile, home broadband and corporate data businesses.
Globe posted consolidated service revenues of P128.99 billion, up 6% from P121.68 billion a year earlier. Nonservice revenues reached P10.35 billion, bringing total gross revenues to P139.34 billion.
Mobile services remained the company's biggest revenue contributor at P91.37 billion, buoyed by a 10% increase in mobile data revenues to P81.22 billion.
Mobile data traffic also rose to 5,705 petabytes from 4,846 petabytes, while average monthly data consumption per subscriber increased to about 17 gigabytes from 15 gigabytes.
Despite the revenue growth, Globe's attributable net income for the first nine months fell 6.9% to P16.47 billion from P17.69 billion a year earlier.

The company attributed the decline to higher net interest expenses and the absence of nonrecurring gains booked in the previous year from tower sales and the dilution of its investment in Mynt Inc., the parent company of GCash.
On a quarterly basis, however, Globe's net income rose 3.6% to P5.44 billion in the July-to-September period from P5.25 billion a year earlier.
Third-quarter gross revenues increased 5.2% to P46.68 billion, supported by stronger business performance and gains from the disposal of property and equipment, which helped cushion rising expenses.
Gross expenses for the quarter also climbed 7.7% to P43.31 billion, driven by higher general, selling and administrative expenses, depreciation and finance costs.
Looking ahead, Globe president and CEO Carl Raymond Cruz said the company was maintaining a cautious outlook amid persistent economic pressures.

“As we enter the final quarter, we are mindful of the persistent inflationary pressures and tighter household budgets, which could weigh on consumer spending and Globe’s overall performance,” Cruz said.

“Nevertheless, connectivity remains an essential household expenditure, and we are encouraged by the prospect of stronger seasonal demand in the fourth quarter, which could help mitigate these pressures and support our growth momentum,” he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Manila to host world leaders for 49th ASEAN summit
articles.summary: Southeast Asian and other world leaders meet in Manila from Sunday, November 15, for the final summit of the Philippines' year as ASEAN chair, with United States President Donald Trump due to attend…

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 3:20pm

MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian and other world leaders meet in Manila from Sunday, November 15, for the final summit of the Philippines' year as ASEAN chair, with United States President Donald Trump due to attend his country’s “special” meet with the bloc.

Trump will attend the ASEAN-US Special Summit on November 17, the last event of the three-day meeting at the Philippine International Convention Center, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) confirmed on Wednesday, November 11.
Trump, who last visited the Philippines in 2017 for the ASEAN summit in Manila during his first term, is scheduled to travel to China afterward for the APEC Summit in Shenzhen.
Uncertain fate for the Code of Conduct
One of the most anticipated efforts during the Philippines’ term as ASEAN chair was its campaign to conclude the long-stalled negotiations for the South China Sea Code of Conduct.
The Palace has been mum about whether the code would be concluded before the end of 2026, the deadline that ASEAN’s foreign ministers previously set themselves.
If the final terms of the document are not ironed out by then, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Singapore takes over ASEAN's leadership.

ASEAN and China first pledged to work toward a code in a non-binding declaration signed in 2002. The code is meant to stop incidents at sea, such as repeated standoffs between Chinese and Philippine vessels, from turning into armed conflict.
But observers say Beijing has repeatedly blocked proposals to make the COC legally binding and enforceable as they prefer a weaker framework that carries no penalties for violations.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is not expected in Manila. The DFA has said Premier Li Qiang has "customarily led the Chinese delegation to Asean-related summits in recent years," but it had not received official confirmation of his attendance as of last week.
The Myanmar problem
Myanmar will be represented by the director-general of its foreign ministry's ASEAN affairs department.
ASEAN has kept Myanmar's leaders out of its summits since the military ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in 2021.
The junta later held a tightly restricted election that made military chief Min Aung Hlaing a civilian president. ASEAN however has withheld recognition of that election.
ASEAN has postponed Myanmar's turn to chair the bloc. That turn would have been this year, which the Philippines had assumed instead.
Leaders of nine other ASEAN members will join Marcos, including Timor-Leste, which was admitted as the bloc's 11th member last year.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and the International Monetary Fund will speak at the plenary as guests of the chair.
The summit opens on Sunday with plenary and retreat sessions, where leaders will review the Philippine chairship and discuss Myanmar.
Leaders will also meet ASEAN lawmakers, business groups and youth representatives.
Separate summits with Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, the United Nations and the United States run from November 16 to 17.
New Zealand will send its deputy prime minister and foreign minister, and Russia its foreign minister.
On November 17, Marcos will also chair the 29th ASEAN Plus Three Summit with China, Japan and South Korea, and the 21st East Asia Summit.
The Philippines expects to present the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, the world's first binding region-wide deal on the digital economy.
Malacañang has declared November 16 to 18 special non-working days in Metro Manila to ease traffic and secure delegates.

articles.title: Marcos trust, performance ratings fall; Sara Duterte hold steady in OCTA Q3 survey
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. saw a decline in his trust and performance ratings while Vice President Sara Duterte's ratings held steady in the latest OCTA Research Group survey.

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 3:15pm
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. saw a decline in his trust and performance ratings while Vice President Sara Duterte's ratings held steady in the latest OCTA Research Group survey.
Based on OCTA's Tugon ng Masa noncommissioned survey, the results of which were released Wednesday, Marcos' trust rating declined from 49% in July to 45% in September.
His distrust rose from 32% to 36%, while 19% remained undecided.
The President's performance rating also fell from 47% in July to 44% in September, while his dissatisfaction increased from 33% to 36%.
"This is the second consecutive quarterly decline in both ratings, following a brief rebound in March 2026, and the fourth decline in the last five survey rounds," OCTA explained.
"Since July 2025, his trust rating has fallen by 19 points (from 64%) and his performance rating by 18 points (from 62%)," it added.
The survey showed that Balance Luzon remains the only major area where he holds majority ratings, at 54% trust and 55% satisfaction.
Marcos' lowest ratings were recorded in Mindanao with 28% trust and 27% satisfaction.
By socioeconomic class, Class E gives him his highest ratings, at 59% trust and 55% satisfaction.
Palace reaction
In a statement, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the survey serves as a reminder but does not show the true work of the President.

"Ang mga tao na naabot na ng gobyerno tulad ng mga magsasaka, mga pasyenteng nakaranas ng zero balance billing sa mga hospital ay maaaring hindi nakasama sa mga survey kaya iba iba ang numerong lumalabas sa mga survey," Castro said.

(People who have already been provided assistance by the government such as farmers, patients who experienced zero balance billing in hospitals may not have been included in the surveys, so the numbers that appear in the surveys are different.)

"Dahil ang mga nagbago ang kondisyon sa Walang Gutom program ay maganda ang nabigay na numero. Anumang numero ang lumabas ay hindi magpapatigil at magpapatinag sa ating pangulo sa pagtatrabaho," she added.
(Because those whose conditions have changed in the Walang Gutom program, the numbers given are good. Whatever number comes out will not stop and sway our president from working.)
Sara Duterte
Meanwhile, Duterte's trust rating slightly increased from 47% to 48%, while distrust remain unchanged at 33%.
Her performance rating also went up from 45% to 46% while the dissatifaction remained at 36%.
"These small gains are within the margin of error and do not yet amount to a recovery," OCTA said.
It added that Duterte's performance rating fell in two successive quarters from 54% in December 2025 to 50% in March and 45% in July 2026.
Meanwhile, her trust rating fell by 8 points between March and July, from 55% to 47%.
"Her September ratings remain just above the series lows recorded in July," OCTA said.
"Beneath the steady national figures, her trust rose by 12 points in NCR and 8 points in the Visayas, but fell by 7 points in Class ABC and 11 points in Class E," it added.
The survey revealed that Duterte continues to enjoy very high ratings in Mindanao at 94% trust and 88% performance and majority ratings in the Visayas at 66% trust and 60% performance.
However, her ratings are much lower in NCR, at 40% trust and 24% satisfaction, and in Balance Luzon, at 25% on both measures.
The survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,200 adult Filipinos from September 28 to October 4, 2026.

It has ±3% margin of error at a 95% confidence level. Subnational estimates for the geographic areas covered in the survey have margins of error of ±6% for NCR, Balance Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, also at a 95% confidence level. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: No board resolution? Kapunan questions 4th defense witness' authority
articles.summary: The prosecution panel questioned the capacity of the defense panel's fourth witness to testify, citing an alleged lack of authorization from the corporation.

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 3:10pm
Prosecution lawyer Lorna Kapunan during the 42nd day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution panel questioned the capacity of the defense panel's fourth witness to testify, citing an alleged lack of authorization from the corporation.

On the 42nd day of the impeachment trial against Vice President Sara Duterte on November 11, prosecution lawyer Lorna Kapunan objected to defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular's offer of testimony that lawyer Suzette Balucanag-Punay is the in-house counsel for both Gencorp Industries Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corporation.

Kapunan argued that without a duly authorized board resolution or secretary's certificate specifically permitting Punay to appear, testify and identify corporate documents in the impeachment trial, her authority to do so is legally absent.

“The board resolution is important because we do not want or this is not to prevent the testimony of the witness, but we do not want at some point in time that she will call the attention of the honorable presiding officer, or hide behind the lawyer-client privilege,” Kapunan explained.
Gular, however, objected, saying that Punay’s appearance was compelled by a subpoena issued by the Senate.
He added that the prosecution's concerns regarding the lawyer-client privilege were "premature.”
"Her appearance today is by virtue of a subpoena...In other words, her appearance today is in compliance with the authority of this honorable [court]," Gular said.

Kapunan then requested that the defense be required to present a board resolution or secretary's certificate affirming Punay's authority within the day or the week, while reserving the prosecution's right to raise the issue.
Meanwhile, Senate Impeachment Presiding Officer Francis Escudero allowed Punay’s testimony under her oath as a lawyer and officer of the court.
However, the court cautioned that by testifying about the corporations, Punay would be presumed to have waived any lawyer-client privilege between her and the companies.

“Her appearance here is duly authorized and that privilege if any between her and the corporation, she will be testifying to has been waived by the client, and that and that she cannot choose when to invoke privilege and when not to invoke privilege as to these two clients of hers, the companies,” Escudero said.
According to the law, a board resolution is a formal document that serves as evidence of the actions and matters taken up by the corporation's directors during a duly held meeting.
This means that a board resolution is necessary for an individual to act on behalf of a corporation.
Punay is the fourth defense witness in Duterte’s impeachment trial under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.
Article II covers allegations involving Duterte's alleged ill-gotten wealth and failure to fully disclose her assets and liabilities in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

articles.title: Lending to property investors falls at record pace, as Australians fall behind on home loans
articles.summary:
Share of CBA customers struggling to repay their mortgages has climbed to 12-year high

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: New lending to property investors fell at its fastest pace on record through the three months to September, as landlords adjust to higher taxes against a backdrop of plunging property prices and rising interest rates.
The latest figures come as the country’s biggest lender, the Commonwealth Bank, reported that the share of its customers struggling to repay their mortgages had climbed to a 12-year high.

As Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, was again forced to defend his budget reforms, CBA’s quarterly trading update showed the share of borrowers 90 days or more behind on their repayments lifted from 0.73% of total lending, to 0.8%.
The last time arrears rates were higher was in 2014, according to previous trading updates.
Nathan Zaia, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said rising arrears rates were happening across the banking sector, and that they “probably hadn’t peaked”.
“Looking at arrears and people falling behind on their home loans, the trend has definitely been picking up,” Zaia said.
But the recent increase was from a low base, he said.
“We’ve had a long period of uncharacteristically very low arrears rates, so it’s not unexpected that they are starting to drift higher.”

Nico de Lange, the director of financial institution ratings at S&P Global, said that despite rising arrears, “it doesn’t look like there is any significant stress coming through” for the banking sector as a whole.
“Obviously after the five rate interest rate increases this year, we are watching things pretty closely,” de Lange said.

The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showed the value of new investor loans plunged by nearly a third in the September quarter – the biggest drop in official records stretching back to 2002.
That was nearly double the previous biggest quarterly fall, the ABS said.

Mish Tan, the head of finance statistics at the ABS, said the data “suggests that investor activity is being influenced by factors beyond increasing borrowing costs, including the potential impacts of tax changes and expectations of lower house prices”.
The Albanese government in the May budget announced changes to the tax on capital gains for investors, and banned negative gearing for new landlords buying an existing home.
As investor appetite for housing collapsed by more than 30%, new lending to owner-occupiers fell by a more sedate 5.3% as part of an overall quarterly drop of 15% in new loans.
after newsletter promotion

The ABS data also showed lending to first home buyers dropped in the quarter by 8.6%, suggesting rising interest rates and worries about the trajectory of property prices were keeping would-be homeowners on the sidelines – if not to the same degree as investors.
Bu Chalmers said the ABS figures also showed falling competition for first-time buyers as investors fled the market.
“Our tax reforms are all about helping more first home buyers into the housing market and we expect to see those benefits play out over years, not months,” he said.
“Because of our reforms, first home buyers will have to compete less with established investors for limited existing housing stock, and we’re starting to see that in this data.”
The number of new loans to investors to build a home was down 12% in the quarter, the ABS figures showed.
The Coalition has promised to repeal the investor tax changes were it to win government.
Andrew Bragg, the shadow housing minister, said: “Labor’s higher housing taxes are discouraging investment when Australia desperately needs more homes”.
“It is time these taxes were repealed before they do any more damage,” Bragg said.

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte didn't participate in Metro City Chow's transactions -- witness
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte has no participation in the transactions of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation from 2022 to 2025 despite being listed as a director and member of the company"s compensation…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 2:57pm

Vice President Sara Duterte has no participation in the transactions of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation from 2022 to 2025 despite being listed as a director and member of the company’s compensation committee, a defense witness said Wednesday.

Atty. Suzette Balucanag-Punay, in-house counsel for Gencorp Industries, Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corporation, said this on the 42nd day of the impeachment trial during her direct examination by defense counsel Justin Gular.
According to the witness, the Vice President is one of the incorporators of Metro City Chow, which operates a fast food chain branch based in Davao City.
Citing General Information Sheets from 2022 to 2025, she also confirmed that Duterte is a member of the Board of Directors and a member of the compensation committee of Metro City Chow.
She also noted that Duterte has a 20% shareholdings in the corporation equivalent to a subscribed capital of P50,000 and paid up capital of P12,500.
Gular then asked the witness of the possible involvement of the Vice President in the business, meetings, or transactions of the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow from 2022 to 2025.
“She did not participate…I have not seen her in the meetings, either Board meetings or even company parties, even in the store, in the branch,” Punay said.
The witness also claimed that Duterte does not participate in the decision making process, the operational management, nor in the administration of the properties of the company.
“What is her participation or involvement in the finances of that corporation, in its transactions, banking, etc,. if any?” Gular asked.
“She has no participation, sir,” Punay answered.
Asked by the defense counsel how the witness knew, she explained, “Because I have attended meetings, I have attended board meetings also and she is not there.”
Punay also expressed belief that Duterte does not receive any compensation or honorarium while being member of the compensation committee of Metro City Chow.

The defense is currently presenting evidence and witnesses for Article II of the impeachment case against Duterte alleging her unexplained wealth due to supposed failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.
articles.summary: Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

image.caption: The average human brain consumes about 20% of the body's energy despite making up only around 2% of its weight. Interestingly, that stays roughly stable whether you are resting or busy with a complex task.Image: Irina Romanova/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps, and running other background processes.
Your brain has its own version of that.
Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?
Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.
It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people, and connecting ideas.
That's your brain's default mode network (DMN).
An accidental find: The discovery of the default mode network
Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.
But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.
So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

blocks.caption: In early brain imaging, rest was often treated less as the object of study than as the baseline researchers compared tasks against. Once scientists began treating that "empty" baseline as meaningful in itself, resting-state neuroscience took off.Image: Maxim Pavlov/Zoonar/IMAGO

blocks.text: And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.
This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.
What does the default mode network do?
The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.
But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.
How your brain switches from DMN to focus on external tasks
There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"
Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.
In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network (SN).

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.
But it's not an on/off switch.
The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.
And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning, or other people.
How notifications and push alerts affect our brain
Smartphones and the brain: Are we crowding out boredom?
Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.
So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?
Maybe, but, so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.
What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching, and disrupt sleep.
And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.
The dark side of the DMN: Rumination, depression and Alzheimer's
The DMN is not always necessarily good.
When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.
But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.
In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.
How to protect your brain's default mode network
Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. Sleep loss and stress have direct evidence for disrupting DMN-related connectivity.
Take real quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.
Embrace boredom and enjoy doing nothing.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.
Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.
You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

articles.title: NCRPO: No threat ahead of ASEAN Summit, maximum tolerance for protests
articles.summary: The National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) on Wednesday said it had not monitored any active security threats ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, as it assured the public that…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 2:55pm

The National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) on Wednesday said it had not monitored any active security threats ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, as it assured the public that police would exercise maximum tolerance toward protesters.
NCRPO officer-in-charge Police Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano said the police intelligence community continued to monitor possible threats as authorities prepared for the international gathering.
“So far, patuloy ang monitoring ng ating intelligence community at ang report sa atin na wala naman pong active na banta,” Abrahano told GTV’s Balitanghali in an interview.
(So far, our intelligence community continues to monitor the situation, and our reports indicate that there is no active threat.)
He said the NCRPO had prepared contingency plans to address possible unforeseen incidents.
Security monitoring would cover summit venues, hotels designated as billeting areas for foreign leaders and delegates, their travel routes and other areas in Metro Manila.
Abrahano also said the police were prepared to handle possible protest actions during the summit.

He said authorities recognized the public's right to express their advocacies and would exercise maximum tolerance while ensuring the safety and security of summit venues, including the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC).
“Asahan po na ang kapulisan ay magbabantay and we will exercise maximum tolerance pero papanatilihin po namin na safe and secure din 'yung mga venue areas natin tulad no'ng sa PICC,” he said.
(Expect the police to be on guard and exercise maximum tolerance, while ensuring that our venue areas, including the PICC, remain safe and secure.)
Abrahano said the NCRPO had not received information as of Wednesday about any permits issued by local government units for protest activities.
District directors and station commanders had been instructed to ensure that gatherings and protests would be held in designated freedom parks.
He urged groups planning to stage protests to cooperate with authorities to help ensure a safe and secure summit.
Meanwhile, Abrahano said security operations would be intensified around designated exclusion zones, including the PICC, where checkpoints and other security measures would be put in place.
The NCRPO was also coordinating with local government units and private security agencies to secure 16 hotels designated as billeting areas for foreign delegates.
Ceremonial lanes had likewise been designated along routes connecting the airport, the billeting areas and the PICC.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: India: CPCB addresses stark Delhi pollution data gap on Diwali night
articles.summary: India's main pollution monitor has issued a clarification on a wide air quality data gap between official and private reporting in New Delhi that saw the city choked amid Diwali fireworks. DW has the…

blocks.text: Live

blocks.text: What you need to know
Following are the latest developments from Indian on Wednesday, November 11

items: India's anti-pollution watchdog said its analyzers are calibrated to measure particulate matter only within a specified range
The CPCB said its air quality monitoring methodology is under review
India and France discuss cooperation in space, critical technology and economic security

blocks.text: November 11, 2026
Delhi air pollution: Central body says air quality data gap due to methodology 'differences' not 'underreporting'

India's Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has issued a clarification on data gap concerns in New Delhi after pollution monitoring in the capital came under scrutiny on Diwali night with official data showing a much lower Air Quality Index (AQI) than private platforms and reports saying that several of the city's monitoring stations went blank.

Celebrations during the Hindu festival of Diwali on Sunday blanketed New Delhi and other surrounding areas in a dense and toxic smog as revelers defied a firecracker ban, adding to the region's seasonal pollution woes.

As smoke and particulate matter from the fireworks kept being released into Delhi's air, an alarmingly wide difference was seen in air pollution figures between official government data and the numbers on private websites and applications.
The CPCB's app showed the AQI at 400 on Diwali night while numbers on private platforms breached the 2,000 mark.

The difference in AQI values was "attributable to differences in measurement of pollutant concentration and in methodology, and not to underreporting," the CPCB said in a statement on X, published Tuesday night.

The anti-pollution watchdog further added that analyzers under its National Air Quality Index (NAQI) reporting methodology, introduced in 2015, were calibrated to measure particulate matter levels of only up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre.
Air quality monitors blackout

Indian media outlets this week reported that several of the capital's 59 to 60 air pollution monitoring stations went dark on the festival of lights and stopped giving data, when pollution was at its peak in the night.

The Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), one of the agencies that operate the capital's monitoring stations, later released the missing data which showed one area of the city witnessing an hourly PM 2.5 concentration of 3,744 micrograms per cubic metre late on Diwali night.

The level was 60 times the national average but CPCB said the readings were not used to calculate the AQI as "the designed system of automated data validation treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range."

"During extreme episodes, which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the body said.
The CPCB went on to say that it is reviewing its existing methodology, considering the advancements in monitoring technology and international practice.
"Internal deliberations and consultations with respect to processing of data beyond system design range are underway," it said.

articles.title: Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains
articles.summary: Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

image.caption: Denmark was an early adopter of wind energy and is now a climate action leaderImage: Steffen Trumpf/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Columbia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the defeat of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."
The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.
Middle East conflict is firing up China's electric future

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.
G20 countries perform particularly poorly
Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.
A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

blocks.caption: Oil exploration in the USA which is the second-worst performer in the CCPI ranking Image: ConocoPhillips/AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. Iran, the United States, Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada all languish at the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in at 53rd.
China a renewable leader but has the world's highest emissions

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

blocks.caption: China is installing renewables at record rates Image: VCG/IMAGO

blocks.text: Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.
The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: How AI worsens online violence against Middle East women
articles.summary: Women in the Middle East already have to deal with an above-average share of online harassment and violence. The proliferation of AI-enabled tools is making it worse.

image.caption: In Syria, young women's rights activists say their private pictures are being stolen from social media, then used against themImage: picture-alliance/dpa

blocks.text: It happens all the time, says Kholoud al-Ameri, an Iraqi journalist and the editor of a news website.

"Female journalists here are often getting messages, and mostly from men," she explains. "They somehow find you online and then they say they just want to talk or they want to add you on Instagram or Facebook," says al-Ameri, who also heads a network of female journalists working on climate change stories. "Sometimes it's hard because the men say they're our readers and we don't want to discourage them. But I usually tell the women just to block these guys."

Syrian activist Yaman Amer tells of similar experiences as a result of writing about women's rights online — she says she gets hundreds of critical comments. "When I talk about women's rights online in a patriarchal society, that's just how things are," Amer, who is studying to be a lawyer in Damascus, told DW. "Not that I accept it. Out of every thousand offensive comments, there's usually one or two that make me feel like I have to report them because they're particularly vile. As in, they're extremely vulgar or threatening. And then it's more than just harassment. It's on a whole other level, humiliating and degrading."
Above-average abuse

Online harassment of women isn't unusual anywhere. Studies by a variety of organizations show that somewhere between 40% and 60% of all women worldwide have experienced it, while 65% have witnessed it.

There is no single standard for assessing the level of online harassment because surveys often use different types of questions or research methods. But in general, women around the Middle East appear to be dealing with a higher-than-global-average level of what is known as "technology facilitated gender-based violence," or TFGBV.

The United Nations Population Fund defines TFGBV as a harmful act "that is committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified ... by the use of information communication technologies," or other digital tools, "against a person on the basis of their gender."
According to research by UN Women, the UN body dedicated to gender equality, 68% of women in the Middle East have had to deal with it, while almost all — close to 100% — have seen it online.

In a 2025 study, UN Women found that 49% of women using the internet in the Middle East don't feel safe from online harassment. The number goes up to almost 70% if the women are more publicly visible activists, journalists or politicians.
And it is already clear that the increased availability of artificial intelligence-powered applications is making online harassment worse.

AI has the potential to supercharge this kind of abuse, the UN Women briefing points out, "both by facilitating the spread of targeted disinformation as well as the proliferation of image-based abuse and deepfake pornographic videos."
Of the women who had experienced online violence while working, around a quarter had already identified "abuse that was generated or amplified by AI tools," the briefing said.

blocks.caption: Iraq elections: In 2018, two female candidates were confronted with sex tapes. Both said the tapes were faked but one withdrew from the election anywayImage: Ismael Adnan Yaqoob/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: AI makes abuse easier

The potential for using the latest technology in order to harass people online has always been there, says Siddharth Venkataramakrishnan, an analyst at the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), which investigates extremism. "But it's just become easier to produce harmful content at scale and in a hyper-targeted way. And the production of non-consensual imagery is a real marker of the democratization of that technology, so it's moving away from primarily targeting celebrities to just regular people."

Venkataramakrishnan has been researching incidents that occurred at the beginning of 2026 when Grok, the AI-powered chatbot belonging to Elon Musk's company SpaceXAI, became able to alter photographs to depict a fully dressed subject as nearly naked. The scandal caused Grok's services to be restricted but, as Venkataramakrishnan pointed out, safeguards across different AI models tend to be inconsistent and users can still find work-arounds to get similar results.

In conservative cultures in the Middle East, the threat of this kind of half-naked picture of a woman being published has serious real-life implications, mostly because of what is and isn't acceptable for women around the region.
What makes the increase in AI-generated fakes even more problematic in the Middle East is that online abuse also has a higher chance of having offline effects.
"Norms related to honor, family reputation and male control can turn digital abuse into real-world consequences," a June briefing by the World Bank notes.
Women in Germany fight back against digital harassment
Lack of specific laws

It's also often not easy for people targeted with this kind of abuse to find legal protection or even somewhere to report it. While some Middle Eastern countries have cybercrime laws, most don't specifically address gender-based online violence nor have they been updated to grapple with AI-related abuse.

Last year's UN Women survey found that 36% of women said they were just told to ignore the online violence, while 23% were blamed for it themselves and 12% were subjected to physical punishment by their families because of it.

Other studies indicate that only about 7% of women who experienced technology-facilitated violence later report it to law enforcement. Various concerns stop them from doing so, including having to present sexualized images or answer personal questions in front of strangers — often also anathema to many women in the region.

The women who had experienced online harassment said they would often just block the perpetrators and around a quarter said they then became more careful about what they posted online. Twenty percent deleted their accounts or left social media altogether.

blocks.caption: In socially conservative contexts, reporting online abuse to authorities might expose the complainants to more 'social stigma or secondary harm from family and community,' UN Women says Image: Farooq Azam/DW

blocks.text: Conflict situations
The rapid growth in AI-enabled harassment can also be more problematic in the Middle East because of the situations the women targeted find themselves living in.

Displacement, war, conflict and instability can all make women more vulnerable to online abuse and exploitation. Even the rapid development of AI-related technologies in a country without corresponding legal guardrails or digital literacy can increase the risk.
For example, observers point out that Saudi Arabia, a generally conservative country with strict rules for female behavior, is going through an accelerated program of digital transformation.

And in Syria, after the ousting of the dictatorial Assad regime, many Syrians "rushed into social media to speak freely," journalist Zaina Erhaim wrote for the Arab Reform Initiative in July this year.

Previously. digital polices had been closely policed by Syria's dictator and a political post could see the writer thrown in jail. But now Syrians "are navigating this newfound liberty without guardrails, oversight or protection," Erhaim argues, and female activists are paying a high price for it, especially where "gender intersects with sect."

In a policy paper published in May, the Syrian Women's Political Movement explained just how bad online abuse had become. In focus groups with 120 women from all around Syria, the majority of participants agreed that digital abuse had become a way of shutting them up. Younger activists reported personal pictures were being stolen from social media, then used against them.

"Smear campaigns targeting women's 'honor' and systemic defamation are actively deployed as punitive measures against any women who attempt to express a critical political opinion," the organization wrote, arguing that what was needed was a law that criminalized digital violence.

If you or someone you know have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help (https://lila.help) lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country around the world.
Women push for political power and equality in new Syria

articles.title: One Nation Victoria candidate apologises for slew of offensive comments about lesbians, Indians and Julia Gillard
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Chris Moore, running for the party in Greenvale, made derogatory social media comments between 2010 and 2012

  • Get our

blocks.text: A One Nation candidate in Victoria has apologised for a series of offensive comments including repeated references to Australian-Indians as “curry munchers”, comparing a woman in burqa to a bag of rubbish, and sharing an image calling Julia Gillard a slut.

The party’s candidate for Greenvale on Melbourne’s north-western fringe, Chris Moore, also made derogatory comments about lesbians and refugees and once posted that he “doesn’t like the way the new homo cleaner at work looks at me”.
One Nation Victoria has not disendorsed the candidate over the comments, which were made on his personal Facebook page between 2010 and 2012.
In a statement, Moore told Guardian Australia “these were unthoughtful posts I shared as a young man among close friends”.
“They don’t reflect who I am today,” Moore said. “Today I’m focused on doing the right thing by the voters of Greenvale, and giving them a strong voice in the Victorian Parliament.”
In 2012, Moore shared a picture of a woman and a child both wearing a burqa and standing between two full plastic rubbish bags. He then posted: “Haha spot the difference.”

Moore also shared an image of Gillard and the Home and Away character Alf Stewart. The image of Gillard was accompanied by the caption: “smash my box Alf!” The image of Stewart was accompanied with: “If I wanted a greasy red box I’d go to KFC ya slut.”

Moore also posted saying he “should probably stop shouting ‘Curry Muncher’ at the TV when I’ve got Indians living next door”. He also posted that he “wonders who does the dishes in a lesbian relationship?”
In 2010 he posted: “Just got the curry munchers to wash his car and pretty happy with the way it came up, looks like the boat people are good for something after all?”
Greenvale is a fairly safe Labor seat with a margin of 7.1%. It is held by Iwan Walters, a parliamentary secretary for multicultural affairs.
The electorate has a large Islamic and West Asian population. It has one of the highest proportions of people born in the Middle East and the lowest share of people with no religion.
At the last election, there was a swing of almost 15% against Labor on a two-party preferred basis.

On Tuesday, One Nation Victoria disendorsed its candidate for Preston, Franco Guardiani, whose private social media account described Adolf Hitler as the “GOAT” and claimed that “importing Islam is making pedophilia legal”.
after newsletter promotion
The party’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, said Guardiani was disendorsed as soon as the comments were confirmed.
“At a time when Jewish Australians are experiencing unprecedented persecution, we are appalled that these comments have been made,” Pickering said.
Guardiani said he was disappointed by the party’s decision to dump him but understood their decision.

One Nation also disendorsed its candidate for the seat of Melbourne, Matthew Collins, over now-deleted comments on social media regarding a number of issues including sexual consent and pornographic jokes. Collins has apologised for the comments.

It is unclear how these candidate’s personal social media histories were not detected during candidate selection and vetting processes. The party has claimed to have invested time and money into improving this process.

In Victoria, One Nation candidates must provide their personal social media accounts for vetting. They are also interviewed by a three-person selection panel including Pickering and two party officials.

articles.title: Woman in Saudi Arabia sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage
articles.summary:
Rights groups condemn reported punishment of Kenyan migrant worker as an ‘act of violence’

A Kenyan mother in Saudi Arabia has reportedly been sentenced to 100 lashes after giving birth…

blocks.text: A Kenyan mother in Saudi Arabia has reportedly been sentenced to 100 lashes after giving birth outside marriage.

Under the Saudi sharia law system, sex outside marriage is a criminal offence. But it is women who are disproportionately targeted, say rights groups, which have condemned the punishment as an “act of violence”.

Although many unmarried women give birth in Saudi Arabia, rights groups say the Kenyan mother’s case only came to light because she had been taken to a hospital, which are required to report single women giving birth to the authorities.
“Most of them give birth at home, that’s why they aren’t reported,” said Ekaterina Porras Sivolobova, founder of Do Bold, a non-profit organisation advocating for migrant workers’ rights in the Gulf.

The Kenyan mother, Esther Wanja Muthoni, was a domestic worker recruited to work as housekeeper and nanny in Saudi Arabia. She reportedly became pregnant during a brief relationship with an Egyptian man and said that the child’s father had since left the country.

A 2024 Guardian investigation found a number of Kenyan single mothers were abandoned by their children’s fathers out of fear of being arrested for having extramarital sex. After the ruling, which was issued last month, Muthoni told the New York Times she was afraid about not being able to endure the lashes and said: “I don’t deserve this.”

The case comes as a planned visit to Saudi Arabia by Reem Alsalem, the UN special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, was postponed last week. Alsalem said she had intended to “raise the situation of specific cases during the visit. If the visit does not take place soon, I will do so separately through the established channels that we have as mandate holders.”

Maryam Aldossari, acting director at the UK-based rights organisation ALQST (al-qist means “justice” in Arabic), said the ruling was an act of violence and the woman should have been sent back to Kenya and not punished.

“It just shows the hypocrisy behind so-called Saudi reform. We know MBS [Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince] has been trying to show the world that Saudi is becoming a modern country that empowers women, yet we see the court sentence a mother to 100 lashes,” said Aldossari.

In April 2020, Saudi announced a reform to end flogging as a judicial punishment. However, it only applied to ta’zir offences, where judges have discretion over punishments. Although most flogging sentences fell into this category, flogging remained a possible punishment for certain hudud (fixed punishments under Islamic law) offences, such as alcohol consumption and adultery, ALQST said in a report in 2021.

Sivolobova said it had been difficult to help in cases involving Kenyan mothers compared with those from other countries. “I haven’t been able to get help from the Kenyan authorities to support these women,” she said.
The Saudi government was approached for comment.

articles.title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment
articles.summary:
Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort

Ukraine says it has captured its first…

blocks.text: Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.

The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.

According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.

A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.

Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.

The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.

The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.
