articles.title: Thousands without shelter face lethal conditions in storm-hit Gaza as they wait for 150,000 tents
articles.summary:
Charities warn of lack of protection amid health fears for more than 940,000 displaced people living in flood-prone areas

Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been left in waterlogged and…

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms at the weekend, while 150,000 new shelters are held outside Gaza awaiting Israeli approval to enter, aid agencies have said.

At least four Palestinian children and woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents. Thousands have been left without shelter and sanitation infrastructure has been destroyed, with sewage spewing into people’s tents.
“All our clothes were soaked. My kids are all sick and I can’t afford to buy them more clothes,” said Raed Jamal, a displaced Palestinian. “Watching them suffering in the cold is heartbreaking.”

blocks.caption: Storm winds rattles tents for displaced Palestinians on Gaza’s coast

blocks.text: “These conditions are so difficult, the whole night I had to use pots to collect rainwater because it was falling on us.”
He shared videos with the Guardian of his tent shaking in the wind as rain poured through holes in its roof.
Aid workers warn disease will spread rapidly unless families are quickly supplied with new shelters and ways to keep warm.

blocks.caption: Displaced Palestinians repair storm-damaged tents in western Gaza City last week. Photograph: Mohammed Salha/APAImages/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The UK-based charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said it was concerned about a rise in health problems because families were living in flooded tents with nowhere else to go.

“Our medical teams expect to see more respiratory illnesses and other health complications linked to cold, damp and overcrowded conditions, and we fear more children could die from hypothermia, as happened last winter,” said Mai Elawawda, MAP’s communications officer in Gaza.

According to the UN, 940,000 people in Gaza are in areas at risk of flooding in makeshift tents without protection from heavy rainfall. The flooding threat has been heightened as facilities for pumping out storm water are not operating due to a lack of power.

Shelterbox, a charity working in humanitarian crisis zones, said the tents it usually supplies during emergencies have been waiting outside Gaza for almost two years and it has instead been forced to improvise shelters built from tarpaulins and wooden pallets. But even these materials, it says, are being restricted.
“The latest devastating floods impacting displaced people in Gaza demonstrate exactly why more durable improvements to shelter are desperately needed ahead of winter,” said a Shelterbox spokesperson.

“The over-reliance on emergency solutions, rather than building shelters from more robust materials, means that many people are living in shelters that are simply not suitable to withstand the weather conditions that the region experiences and will quickly deteriorate.”

blocks.caption: Palestinians inspect tents buried under rocks and earth a day after a large sandstone slab collapsed at a displacement camp, killing at least five people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: A child drowned in flood waters and at least three children and their mother died when a sand dune fell on their tent at the weekend, according to the Palestinian health ministry.
The UN said 26,000 households had sought its help after the rains and at least 3,900 households were now without shelter at all.

Palestinians in Gaza are facing their second winter since a ceasefire was agreed more than a year ago, but aid workers said conditions were no better than last year because of Israeli restrictions on “dual-use items” and backlogs at crossings were limiting critical supplies to build shelters.

“It’s very difficult to deal with it because there’s also there’s no clear process for things. There’s a level of capriciousness that one day toolkits will be allowed in, another day toolkits will not and they don’t say why,” said Sheltherbox the spokesperson.

The Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu) has called on the British government to pressure Israel to allow supplies into Gaza and reverse restrictions on humanitarian workers, including restoring the licences of dozens of organisations, such as Médecins Sans Frontières, Oxfam and the Norwegian Refugee Council.

blocks.caption: Employees and workers of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) hold placards during a protest in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, 9 November. Photograph: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “The predictable winter rains and floods have, as warned about, battered already devastated Palestinians, where disease and malnutrition is rife, and a basic tent blocked by Israel is a manmade and political scarcity,” said Caabu’s head of parliamentary affairs, Joseph Willits. “A lack of political action isn’t something a Palestinian family trying to shelter from Gaza’s floods can afford.”

Israel claimed last week to have allowed 10,000 tents into Gaza, but that falls far short of the number needed – the UN said 150,000 were waiting outside Gaza for entry for the estimated 94% of Palestinians in Gaza who need help finding shelter.

The Israeli NGO Gisha, which lobbies for goods and people to be able to enter and exit Gaza more freely, said the Israeli authorities had enforced stricter limits on goods entering Gaza than in previous ceasefires.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian child shows the inside of his family’s tent during a storm in Gaza

blocks.text: While the Israeli authorities claim to be allowing an average of 600 trucks into Gaza each day, they count 12 pallets of goods as a single truck, even though a truck usually carries about 20 pallets – which could amount to about a 40% reduction on what could be carried into Gaza. Gisha has also accused Israeli authorities of a lack of transparency on what is being allowed to enter Gaza.

Nour al-Batsh, the mother of a seven-month-old child, said she was forced to rent a partially destroyed apartment she shares with others for $500 a month, relying on donations from abroad, after her tent collapsed.

“The cold is lethal. Living in a tent by the sea means facing the constant threat of death from the freezing temperatures,” said Batsh, who can see her old tent from her current shelter. “We are still in autumn, and winter has not even properly begun. I look at my fragile tent and I beg God that I will not have to go back to it. Because death inside that tent is certain.”

articles.title: Fresh concerns raised over Gaza doctor held by Israel for 23 months without charge
articles.summary:
Independent Israeli professor says Hussam Abu Safiya’s life will be at risk until he receives proper medical treatment

An independent professor who reviewed the medical records of a…

blocks.text: An independent professor who reviewed the medical records of a prominent Gaza doctor held in an Israeli prison without charge for nearly 23 months has raised serious concerns about his health.
Hussam Abu Safiya was detained at work on 27 December 2024 and later held in solitary confinement at Rakefet, a notorious underground prison.

During a visit by a lawyer from Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) in the summer, the doctor told of harsh conditions, untreated medical problems and severe food shortages. Witnesses said he had become almost unrecognisable.
Nearly 700 days after his arrest, Israeli authorities have yet to bring any formal charges against Abu Safiya, who is the director of Kamal Adwan hospital in northern Gaza.
He was classified as an “unlawful combatant” along with more than 375 medical workers – a designation Israel has used to justify prolonged detention without trial.

Last month, Israel’s supreme court rejected a petition to release the doctor. Over the weekend, a district court rejected a separate petition to allow Abu Safiya an independent medical examination, despite troubling findings in his medical records that were not adequately investigated, according to Prof Amit Tirosh, an independent Israeli specialist who reviewed a file obtained by PHRI.

blocks.caption: Hussam Abu Safiya, right, shows a UN delegation around the Kamal Adwan hospital in northern Gaza in September 2024. His family have not been able to communicate with him directly in detention. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: In an interview with the Guardian, Tirosh said Abu Safiya’s weight had fallen from 90kg (14st 2lb) in January 2025 to 76kg this May.
“Continuous food deprivation and weight loss, repeated beatings and injuries, with inadequate medical care, can definitely cost Dr Abu Safiya his life,” Tirosh said.
“According to PHRI records, more than 100 prisoners died in Israeli facilities between 2023 and 2025 … a threat to his life unfortunately cannot be ruled out.”
Tirosh identified insufficient investigation of chest pain, delays in treating scabies and a drop in haemoglobin levels that warranted further examination.

“A 14kg weight loss is very alarming, even more so if the cause is unknown,” he added. “More troubling, the medical team was neither surprised nor concerned: one prison physician wrote that his weight loss over a year is ‘a common trend among security prisoners associated to their diet’.
“Haemoglobin dropped between February and July 2026, long after the weight loss, so detention or starvation alone cannot explain it; it coincided with the reported beatings in Rakefet.
“Such blood loss can be life-threatening and requires urgent ER evaluation. Per the records, these urgent problems were not addressed and could endanger his life.”

Medical records documented bruising around one of Abu Safiya’s eyes, dizziness and rib pain in July. He told his lawyers he had been beaten by prison guards but Tirosh said the records did not explain his injuries.

The district court ruling also revealed allegations made by Israeli authorities that Abu Safiya had exaggerated his medical problems, set up organisations from prison, influenced other prisoners and maintained international contacts.
PHRI said the Israeli allegations did not justify denying him an independent medical examination, a right protected by law.
“The bottom line is that a third party should see him and the full medical records,” said Tirosh. ‘‘Refusing an independent examination is never justified.

“To the Israeli prison system authorities I would say that I feel deep shame to be counted with them as a doctor or health provider in Israel. As a system, they betray every medical and ethical principle I stand for.”
The Israeli prison service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Abu Safiya had become the face of health workers struggling to treat patients throughout the war in Gaza before his detention. He is being held indefinitely, along with thousands of other Palestinian civilians, in prisons that Israeli rights groups say have become torture camps.
At the time of his arrest at work, Abu Safiya was wearing a white medical coat that he had refused to wash since his son, Ibrahim, was killed by a drone strike at the hospital entrance that October.
Abu Safiya had helped keep the hospital running through more than 80 days of siege and attacks by Israeli forces amid an intensive military operation in the surrounding refugee camp.

“Fourteen Palestinian doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, remain imprisoned without charge or trial at a time when Gaza’s healthcare system desperately needs them,” said Naji Abbas of PHRI.

A spokesperson for the Israeli prison service (IPS) told the Guardian the allegations are “part of a broader campaign aimed at discrediting the state of Israel” and that the IPS “operates in accordance with the law and under constant judicial oversight”.
Abu Safiya’s family have not been able to communicate with him directly in detention.

articles.title: Youpla directors disqualified over collapsed funeral fund that targeted Aboriginal families
articles.summary:
Three directors were fined a combined $90,000 in federal court judgment and disqualified from managing a corporation for between five and 10 years

  • Get our

blocks.text: Three directors of a collapsed funeral fund that marketed insurance to Aboriginal families have been banned from managing corporations for at least five years and ordered to pay a combined $90,000 after being found to have breached their duties to clients.

On Wednesday, federal court justice Geoffrey Kennett ordered the former director of the insurance company Youpla Group, previously the Aboriginal Community Benefit Fund (ACBF), Jonathan Law, to pay the commonwealth $50,000 and disqualified him from managing corporations for six years.

Michael Wilson, also a director, was ordered to pay $20,000 and disqualified from managing corporations for 10 years, while director Geoffrey Clayton was ordered to pay $20,000 and disqualified from managing corporations for five years.

The trio were also ordered to pay a combined $17,000 towards plaintiff’s costs. Kennett found they had failed to perform their duties with the degree of “care and diligence” expected, failed to manage conflicts of interest, and caused a detriment to the ACBF members.

It followed a judgment late last month where the founder of the company, Ron Pattenden, was ordered to pay a quarter of a million dollars and barred from managing corporations for 15 years. Pattenden acknowledged he had breached directors’ duties in a claim settlement with financial watchdog, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC).

During the same judgment, the former Youpla Group chief Bryn Jones was found by Kennett to have breached his directorial duties after a contested liability hearing in February. He denied having knowledge of the fund’s insurance premium increases. Jones’s penalty will be determined at a hearing at a later date.
Youpla sold junk funeral policies to Indigenous people across Australia for decades, including targeting communities where English was not the first language and communities with low literacy levels.

It collapsed in March 2022, leaving more than 13,000 Aboriginal people, some elderly and in palliative care, without the means to pay for funerals. Families had to resort to crowdfunding and some were forced to leave their loved ones’ bodies in the morgue while they raised the funds.

In August 2023, Asic commenced proceedings in federal court against the five former directors and officers for breaches of their duties, alleging governance failures and director misconduct that affected the First Nations people who were members of the funds.

It alleged the directors and officers maintained insurance arrangements with Crown Insurance, a Vanuatu-based company owned and controlled by Pattenden and another director, Law, and did not act in the best interest of the ACBF entities and members.
Breaches of directors’ duties can attract a maximum penalty of $200,000 for each breach that occurred between 2017 and March 2019.

Youpla targeted Indigenous people using marketing materials in the distinctive red, black and yellow colours of the Aboriginal flag, including stuffed toys and colouring books for children, turning up to community events and by conducting door-to-door sales.
after newsletter promotion
It was investigated by various regulators over the years but it was not until 2018, when its conduct was exposed in the banking royal commission, that its licence to sell new products was withdrawn.
In 2021 Asic questioned its solvency, and the company’s directors finally pulled the plug.

The federal court handed Youpla a $1.2m fine in September 2023 for misrepresenting junk funeral policies, finding it had told plan holders they would receive a lump sum payment when in fact they would only be reimbursed for expenses they could prove had been incurred.
Youpla avoided paying millions more in fines handed down by the federal court in July 2025 because it was in liquidation.
A $97m federal government support package was announced in February 2024 to help thousands of mostly low-income Aboriginal families recover from financial loss.

The government’s payments to remaining victims will continue to be processed until 1 December this year. Eligible recipients have the choice of a funeral bond or a cash payment worth 60% of the value of their policy.
– with Australian Associated Press.

image.caption: The windshield of the bus was destroyed after it slammed into the vehicles stopped at a traffic light Image: NEWSIS/Handout/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: A bus triggered a crash involving dozens of passenger cars, a truck, and four other buses in Seongnam, South Korea on Wednesday morning, leaving many injured, according to South Korean authorities.
What do we know so far?

The fire department of Gyeonggi Province, were Seongnam is located, said 57 people were injured, with nine seriously hurt after the bus collided with 32 vehicles and then slammed into a median strip. blocks.caption: The bus came to a stop after hitting a median stripImage: Yonhap/REUTERS

blocks.text: An investigation has been launched into the cause of the collision.

The driver told investigators the brakes on his bus had failed, according to a report by Yonhap news agency. The man, believed to be in his 60s, tested negative in a breathalyzer test. Local media had reported that he was also hospitalized after the crash.
The city of Seongnam, with its population of nearly 900,000, is located just south of the capital metropolis of Seoul. The crash occurred during rush hour traffic.
Dozens of fire personnel and vehicles were deployed to the scene of the crash and a emergency medical station was also set up there.

articles.title: David Jones to close half its stores triggering mass job losses under ‘urgent restructure’
articles.summary:
Australia’s oldest department store collapsed into voluntary administration last week after years of steep losses

David Jones is set to shutter half its department store network, triggering…

blocks.text: David Jones is set to shutter half its department store network, triggering mass job losses under a sweeping restructure, receivers FTI Consulting said on Wednesday.
David Jones employs more than 6,000 staff across 38 stores.
FTI said in a statement that it would proceed with an “urgent restructure of the business”.
“As part of this restructure, the receivers have commenced an immediate consultation process for all staff associated with 19 stores that have been identified for closure,” FTI said.
“For the immediate term these stores will continue trading and while there is no final date for the closures, we anticipate they will cease trading by the end of the year.”
Under a dual appointment, receivers FTI has day-to-day control of operations, while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital.
The upheaval follows years of steep losses after the retailer failed to carve out a profitable niche in a sector disrupted by online competitors and stand-alone upmarket stores.
The department store collapsed into voluntary administration last week.
In documents released late on Tuesday, David Jones’s administrators revealed they reviewed the private equity-owned department chain’s finances months before it fell into administration.
Some small suppliers are owed money dating back to stock sent in April, well before David Jones missed rent payments and fell into administration.
after newsletter promotion

Its private equity owner, Anchorage Capital, has long sought a slimmed down version of David Jones, free from long-term leases on underperforming sites. It is expected to make a proposal to administrators to re-purchase the 188-year-old chain.

The following stores will be closed: Carousel, WA, Garden City, WA, Glen Waverley, VIC, Green Hills, NSW, Hay Street Mall, WA, Highpoint, VIC, Hornsby, NSW, Macarthur Square, NSW, Macquarie Centre, NSW, Malvern Central, VIC, Marion, SA, Newmarket, NZ, Parramatta, NSW, Robina Town Centre, QLD, Sunshine Plaza, QLD, Warringah Mall, NSW, West Lakes, SA, Woden, ACT, Wollongong Central, NSW.

articles.title: Kennedys sue to block Trump's arch, arguing it would cast shadow on JFK's grave
articles.summary: Nine members of the political dynasty say the 250ft structure would cast a shadow on gravesites.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery
The family of former US President John F Kennedy has sued to block construction of a triumphal arch that President Donald Trump plans to build in the nation's capital.

Nine members of the political dynasty argue the 250ft (76m) structure would block the view of Kennedy's grave, as well as the graves of thousands of veterans buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.
Last week, a US judge temporarily halted the project on the heels of a vote allowing construction to proceed.
The White House said it was "unfortunate" to see that some members of the Kennedy family had joined litigation against an arch "intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery".
"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis R Ingle said in a statement to the BBC.
"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.
Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed arch
Last week the project won approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.
But US District Judge Tanya Chutkan then ruled there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch as litigation plays out.

The Kennedy family filed its complaint under a joint lawsuit brought by the state of Virginia and Washington DC seeking to block construction, arguing that the arch will damage "historically significant sightlines" if erected at the gateway of the cemetery.
The plaintiffs include seven children of Robert and Ethel Kennedy, as well as their grandson - former Democrat congressman Joe Kennedy - and Ted Kennedy's son Edward Kennedy Jr.
It does not include Trump cabinet official Robert F Kennedy Jr, who leads the Department of Health and Human Services.
Their motion moves to intervene in two other lawsuits filed by conservationists and veterans seeking to halt the construction.

They say the arch would be a "permanent denigration" of the gravesites and that the Kennedy offspring "would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended".

blocks.caption: Satellite image with 3D buildings visible showing a model of the proposed Triumphal Arch in Washington DC, positioned south of the Potomac River at the end of Arlington Memorial Bridge. The Lincoln Memorial, on the other side of the bridge, the Washington Monument, further to the east, and the Wh…

blocks.text: The Kennedy family argues the structure "will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family's honor" at the cemetery.
The structure would also "fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites", including the memorials of hundreds of thousands of US veterans, the Kennedys said.
The complaint said that the National Park Service and Interior Department authorised construction on 5 November 2026 without the necessary congressional approval.
The so-called Arc de Trump is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.
Last year, he also added his name to the Kennedy Center, a major Washington DC cultural institution named in honour of JFK.
Trump's name remained on the facade for six months until the addition was ruled illegal and removed.

articles.title: Israel: Eisenkot proposes October 7 probe as new Knesset sworn in
articles.summary: Ex-IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot has yet to forge a coalition that would allow him to replace Benjamin Netanyahu, despite the new Knesset being dominated by the critics of the current prime minister.

image.caption: Eisenkot's coalition also wants to impose term limits on Israeli prime ministersImage: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The parliamentary bloc led by Israeli ex-military leader Gadi Eisenkot announced a slew of initiatives on Tuesday targeting the legacy of current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as the new Israeli Parliament, or Knesset, was sworn in.
Israel held a parliamentary election on October 27.
Eisenkot's bloc wants government inquiry into October 7 attack

Eisenkot's centrist Yashar Party and allied parties are seeking an official government inquiry into the Hamas-led terror attacks on October 7, 2023, which killed some 1,200 people in Israel and resulted in another 251 hostages being taken into Gaza.
The attack, which occurred on Netanyahu's watch, was the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.

Some media outlets had reported that Netanyahu received warnings from Egypt and the UAE ahead of the October 7 assault. The Israeli prime minister denied the claims and said he would sue for defamation over the publications.

In addition to an October 7 probe, the anti-Netanyahu opposition is also seeking to impose term limits on the office of prime minister and aims to reverse the controversial efforts made by the Netanyahu government to reforming the judiciary. Eisenkot's bloc is also seeking to depose Knesset speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally.

blocks.caption: The new Knesset has 33 female members — the highest share since Israel's founding in 1948Image: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP

blocks.text: "We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment," Eisenkot said prior to the swearing-in of the new Knesset. He pledged to "form a national-emergency government as quickly as possible."
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot bloc short of Knesset majority
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has given Eisenkot a mandate to try to form a government within six weeks.
Eisenkot's coalition bloc landed 48 seats in the recent election, whereas Netanyahu's bloc received 53 seats. But neither bloc has enough seats to form a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

Arab parties garnered a record 19 out of 120 seats in the new Knesset. During the swearing-in ceremony, far-right Israeli politician Itamar Ben-Gvir harassed Arab-Israeli lawmaker Yousef Jabareen in the Knesset chamber

Eisenkot's bloc could choose to align with the Arab parties to form a government, but Avigdor Lieberman and his right-wing Yisrael Beitenu party oppose the idea. Yisrael Beitenu, which won seven seats in the new Knesset, is a part of the Eisenkot bloc.
Israeli president asks Eisenkot to form government
Netanyahu urges national unity government to confront Iran

Netanyahu, in a speech to the Knesset, called for a national unity government — a proposal which has been ruled out by Eisenkot. The incumbent head of government lashed out at Arab parties and accused them of backing Israel's destruction while saying the national unity government is necessary to confront Iran.

"In the very near future, we're going to be confronted by international pressure to accept a nuclear-armed Iran and the preservation of this terror regime that seeks to annihilate us," Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot condemned Netanyahu's remarks, whereas Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party, walked out during Netanyahu's speech. The Democrats have eight seats and are part of the Eisenkot bloc.
"Netanyahu is struggling to accept that the Israeli public fired him. Now he is lying and inciting against the Arab public in an attempt to cling to power by force," Golan said on X.
How Israel's PM Netanyahu holds on to power

If Eisenkot fails to form a government, Israeli President Herzog could choose another lawmaker, presumably Netanyahu, to cobble together a coalition. The 77-year-old Netanyahu first took power in 1996 and has had three separate stints as the Israeli head of government.
Netanyahu is now the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history.

articles.summary: Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for…

image.caption: Actor Stacy Keach, seen in a February 2003 photo, has died at the age of 85. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.
Keach died at his home in Poland, following a long battle with heart problems

Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure," his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.

Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favourite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.

Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating World's Most Amazing Videos on TV. He played a deranged colonel in The Ninth Configuration (also known as Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane), led the TV show Titus, had a role in Alexander Payne's Oscar-nominated drama Nebraska and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama Blue Bloods. Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in Jay Kelly.

"My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career," he told New York magazine in 2012. "My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I've gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything."
'One of the greats'

Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie Lone Rider, said in a post on X that Keach was a "consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him."
Keach, seen in April 1984, was one of America's finest stage actors. (Daily Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

Keach played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries Mistral's Daughter, a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz's novel Princess Daisy, Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli's Jesus of Nazareth and Maj. Jonas Steele in The Blue and the Gray. He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds.

Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play Indians, played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in King Lear on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in The Kentucky Cycle in 1993, The Country Wife in 1965 and Other Desert Cities in 2011.

He also headed the national touring company cast of Frost/Nixon, portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with Sleuth with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of King Lear at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for Pamplona, a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run's cancellation.
'Lowest moment' was prison

While he was still doing Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer (later titled The New Mike Hammer), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.
Stacy Keach and his wife Malgosia Tomassi Keach pose for a photo at a premiere in 2006. (Lucas Jackson/The Associated Press)

"As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats," he wrote in his 2013 book, All in All: An Actor's Life On and Off the Stage. He added: "It was the lowest moment of my life."

He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book The Blue and the Gray.

The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.

In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, The Long Riders. He said the experience was "very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity."

After prison, he narrated the TV documentary High on the Job, and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. "There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one's existence," he testified.

Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centres. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the Hammer series. He said he treasured her photos and letters behind bars.
Married 4 times
Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.

His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, Intimate Strangers with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, The Return of Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer, also played well, and then the Mike Hammer series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS' 1986-87 schedule.

Many years later, in the TV series Prison Break that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.
Born in Savannah, Ga., Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.

articles.title: Slovak foreign minister to open embassy in Manila
articles.summary: Slovakia will formally open its embassy in Manila during a visit by Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár on November 12-15, the Department of Foreign Affairs said on Wednesday, November 11.

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 11:16am
Slovakia's Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar looks on during a joint press conference with Poland's Foreign Minister after their meeting at Foreign Ministry building in Warsaw on March 13, 2025.
AFP / Wojtek Radwanski

MANILA, Philippines — Slovakia will formally open its embassy in Manila during a visit by Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár on November 12-15, the Department of Foreign Affairs said on Wednesday, November 11.
During the visit, Blanár will also sign a declaration depositing Slovakia’s instrument of accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, ASEAN’s 1976 peace pact, the DFA said.
It is the first official visit by a Slovak foreign minister to the Philippines since 2015.
Blanár, who is traveling with a business delegation, will also meet Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro on Thursday, November 12.
On Friday, November 13, the minister is set to meet Trade Secretary Cristina Aldeguer-Roque and give the keynote speech at a Philippines-Slovak business forum.

The 1976 treaty commits its parties to respect for sovereignty, the principle of non-interference, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Countries outside the region have been able to join since 1987, but only with the consent of all ASEAN members.
Miloš Koterec, Slovakia’s first resident ambassador, presented his credentials to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in February.
The Philippines and Slovakia established diplomatic relations in 1993.
Lazaro and Blanár last met in April in Brunei, at the ASEAN-EU Ministerial Meeting.

articles.title: Labor won’t scrap ABC and SBC ombudsmen in favour of external body as suggested by antisemitism envoy
articles.summary:
Jillian Segal suggested ‘transferring’ powers in updated report released a fortnight ago but government sources note media regulator already exists

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Albanese government won’t follow a suggestion by the antisemitism envoy to scrap the ABC and SBS ombudsmen and replace them with an external oversight body.

In a list of updated priorities released last month, Segal proposed an “external independent ombudsman” to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of the war in Gaza and to ensure publicly funded broadcasters were “held accountable to their own stated standards of accuracy and impartiality”.

“Many in the Jewish community remain concerned that coverage they perceive as one-directional may contribute to a negative – and even hostile – view by audiences of those who support Israel, or have sympathy for it,” Segal said in her updated plan to combat antisemitism.

Segal said the government should consider “transferring” responsibilities from the ABC and SBS ombudsmen to an “external independent ombudsman consistent with other sectors such as telecommunications and banking”.

The ABC said at the time its complaints process was “the most robust and transparent in the Australian media” and both broadcasters stated they were subject to external review by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (Acma).
This week, government sources noted that Acma already acted as an external independent regulator that could investigate complaints if they needed to be escalated beyond the ABC and SBS ombudsmen.
A spokesperson for the federal communications minister, Anika Wells, on Wednesday thanked Segal for her work and said there was no place for antisemitism in Australia.
It was an evil “that tears at the fabric of our country … [and] puts the peaceful, free and equal society we cherish at risk”, they said.

It is understood Labor could consider changes in response to recommendations from the royal commission into antisemitism that’s scheduled to report in mid-December. The commission, headed by former high court judge Virgina Bell, was established after the antisemitic Bondi beach massacre in December 2025.
“The government will soon receive the final report from the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion,” Wells’ spokesperson said on Wednesday.
“[It] will continue to work with the special envoy, the Jewish community and all Australians to combat antisemitism and strengthen our social cohesion.”
Segal’s latest suggestion regarding the ABC and SBS received a mixed response a fortnight ago.

Alex Ryvchin, the co-chief executive of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, welcomed Segal’s suggestions, warning meaningful oversight of coverage by public broadcasters could only be achieved “through external accountability”.
But the progressive Jewish Council of Australia criticised the envoy’s new plan as “Trumpian”, arguing it threatened freedom of speech and democratic rights.
after newsletter promotion

The Australian Palestine Advocacy Network criticised attempts to conflate legitimate criticism of Israel with antisemitism and stated: “Speaking out against Israel’s ongoing atrocities is the prerogative of anyone who believes in human dignity and human rights.”
Segal in October wrote that the “independence of public broadcasters must, of course, be protected”.

“That independence, however, does not – and should not – amount to a right to be free from external scrutiny and empirical review. Indeed, ensuring that the processes withstand fair scrutiny can only increase confidence.”

The ABC ombudsman has previously investigated public complaints related to coverage of the Middle East and the war in Gaza, including the Israeli president’s visit to Australia and a press club address by the Israeli ambassador.

ABC Alumni, which represents hundreds of former staff, has said that since October 2023 the ABC ombudsman has upheld four out of thousands of complaints of bias or inaccuracy relating to Middle East coverage.

Acma, “to which dissatisfied complainants can appeal, has upheld none,” the group said in a statement, adding it was “outraged at the continued insistence by Jillian Segal … that the ABC and SBS, Australia’s most trusted news outlets, are contributing to antisemitism”.

In her first report in mid-2025, Segal initially proposed the special envoy be given powers to monitor media organisations to encourage “accurate, fair and responsible reporting” to ensure impartiality and balance and to avoid “accepting false or distorted narratives”.
She then told the royal commission into antisemitism in mid-2026 she wanted a new “oversight” committee that could give ABC and SBS coverage a “tick” or “guidance”.
Segal told Senate estimates this week she was concerned about “the tone [and] the frequency of reporting about Gaza from the ABC”.

articles.title: Philippines among 4 countries set for first climate loss and damage fund grants
articles.summary: The Philippines is among four countries whose projects have been cleared for the first grants from an international fund set up to help developing nations recover from climate-related losses and…

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 10:58am
A woman walks along a mud covered street in the aftermath of Typhoon Kalmaegi in Liloan, in the province of Cebu on Nov. 6, 2025.
AFP / Jam Sta. Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is among four countries whose projects have been cleared for the first grants from an international fund set up to help developing nations recover from climate-related losses and damage.

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage is expected to award a total of $92 million in December to projects in Jamaica, Ivory Coast, Nigeria and Haiti. Each project can receive between $5 million and $20 million.
The projects were deemed ready for approval during the fund's board meeting in July in the Philippines, following the submission of 176 requests earlier this year amounting to $2.8 billion.

The fund recently set aside $20 million to help Nepal recover from deadly floods in August. The allocation was a first for the mechanism but required a special request, pressure from developing countries and an extraordinary board meeting.
Georg Børsting, one of the fund's co-chairs, said the decision on Nepal did not necessarily set a precedent for future requests.

"The precedent that was set was that the board proved that it was able to do this type of extraordinary meeting," he told Agence France-Presse shortly before the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) in Turkey.
The fund's other co-chair, Camila Minerva Rodriguez Tavarez, said the mechanism was still determining how to support longer-term recovery efforts.
"We are not an emergency response fund. This is not humanitarian aid," she said.
Wealthy countries have pledged $822 million to the fund since its establishment at COP27 in Egypt in 2022, but no money has yet been disbursed.
Rodriguez Tavarez said the available resources remain far below what vulnerable countries need to recover from climate-related disasters.
"The needs are absolutely in the billions," she said.
Børsting added that a single fund would not be enough to meet the growing demand for assistance. — with a report from Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
articles.summary: The infamous 400 Mawozo gang was targeted by the El Salvador military which has deployed thousands of troops to combat Haiti's gang violence crisis.

blocks.text: The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said.
The infamous 400 Mawozo gang, which is known for kidnappings and intimidation tactics, was targeted in a ground and air attack at a complex on the outskirts of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince.
It is El Salvador's first military action on a Haitian target since it deployed more than 2,000 soldiers there last month, as part of a mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran technicians.
Haiti has been plagued by gang violence for years, with heavily armed groups controlling large parts of the capital, and beyond.
El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced the news on X, external, boasting that most of the gang members fled without trying to fight.
"We destroyed the house of [gang leader] Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters," he wrote on Tuesday.
The post was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex, reportedly in the suburb of Croix-des-Bouquets, the gang's stronghold.
As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

Several media outlets have reported that as many as 20 people were killed, however that has not been confirmed by authorities. There has also been no official confirmation of the extent of the damage at the property, with Haitians questioning whether it has been destroyed or just damaged.
The Miami Herald reports that the gang's leader, Wilson "Lanmò San Jou" Joseph, was not there at the time.
The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the gang's headquarters.
Haiti's National Police drone task force was involved in the attack, supported by Salvadoran soldiers, the Miami Herald reports, citing several sources.

Posting on X after the strikes, Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé thanked the Salvadoran military's commitment "in the fight against gangs", and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority".
"THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!" he added.
Some 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were deployed to Haiti last month after four air force technicians were abducted at gunpoint while food shopping in October.
El Salvador's right-wing president has vowed to bring the men home alive and warned the gang to release them immediately or face sustained pressure from his military.
The four abducted men were working as part of the GSF, made up of troops from several nations, initially led by soldiers from Chad.

President Bukele's move to send thousands of Salvadoran troops to Haiti has raised concerns, with critics saying they are not all working within the command structure of the GSF. It has raised questions about the operational legitimacy and legality of their actions in the Caribbean nation.
Amnesty International has urged both countries to "ensure all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law".
Such concerns do not appear to phase Bukele, however, who continues to directly warn and target the gang leaders.
The attack on the supposed gang headquarters seemingly came after a user on X had urged Bukele to attack the complex.
"Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we'll destroy it," he replied to the post, which has now been taken down, apparently for violating X's rules.
The 400 Mawozo gang is the largest criminal organisation in Haiti, and known for kidnappings, extortion, murders and arms trafficking.
Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and remains largely under gang control.
At least 5,700 people have been killed or injured there by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year alone, the United Nations has said.
El Salvador has recorded huge reductions in gang violence under President Bukele as part of a sweeping crackdown, and he has vowed to do the same in Haiti.

However, human rights groups have argued that the way he has done it is unlawful, with the open-ended extension of emergency laws, the treatment of detainees in El Salvador's high-security mega-prison and the mass trials of alleged gang members.

articles.title: US Republicans derail push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth seems set to survive the impeachment bid launched by maverick Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie, with President Donald Trump praising the outcome of the vote.

image.caption: Hegseth has sought to strike a defiant tone as political pressure mountsImage: Nathan Howard/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US House Republicans voted on Tuesday to effectively block an impeachment bid against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, handing a victory to President Donald Trump as his administration reels from last week's midterm defeat.
Trump praised the outcome online, describing Hegseth as a "Great American Patriot" and saying the effort to impeach the hawkish Pentagon chief "has miserably FAILED!"
Pentagon chief says claims against him 'slander' and 'farce'

Hegseth has been facing increasing political pressure over the Iran war. Yesterday, Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth in an apparent bid to force a vote before the new US Congress convenes in January.

Massie is one of the few prominent Republicans who is also an outspoken Trump critic. The Kentucky congressman accuses the US defense secretary of waging the war illegally and without congressional approval. While the resolution focuses on Iran, it also questions Hegseth's actions regarding the strikes on Houthi rebels in Yemen and military operations in Venezuela.
US Defense Secretary Hegseth faces impeachment over Iran war
Earlier on Tuesday, Hegseth dismissed the accusations as "slander" and "sabotage."
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said at a Pentagon press conference.
Massie: Republicans won't leave a sinking ship
The US House of Representatives has now voted 211 to 204 to refer the initiative to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee for further consideration.
Massie had warned that the referral would effectively kill his impeachment initiative.
What will Democrats do with their midterm mandate?
Following the vote, Massie compared his Republican colleagues in the outgoing Congress to passengers staying on the Titanic.
"They know it's a sinking ship but committed to stay on board," he said.

While Hegseth appears safe from Massie's impeachment initiative, he is expected to face renewed pushback and possibly a new impeachment effort once the Democratic Party takes control of both the House and Senate next year.
